summary: Defines the part of the Management Information Base used to manage Ethernet-like interface types, extending the previous specification. It was replaced by RFC 2665.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of readings you can check on a network cable connection, like speed and errors.

questions: how do i monitor ethernet collisions
subtitle: Standard counters and statistics for managing Ethernet network interfaces.

tldr.problem: Network administrators need a standard way to check the health of Ethernet interfaces, monitoring errors, collisions, and transmission statistics through SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the EtherLike-MIB module with tables of counters for alignment errors, frame check errors, collisions, and other Ethernet-specific measurements that systems can report to management stations.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can monitor the health of Ethernet networks and detect physical layer problems like bad cables or collisions. The RFC was quickly superseded by RFC 2665 to add support for faster 100 Mb/s Ethernet.

today: RFC 2358 was quickly superseded by RFC 2665 in August 1998, which extended the definitions to improve support for 100 Mb/s and faster Ethernet interfaces and provided additional management objects. The core statistics and tables defined here remain largely unchanged in modern Ethernet management.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2358 defines managed objects for Ethernet-like interfaces using the Management Information Base (MIB) framework. It updates RFC 1650 by adding support for 100 Mb/s Ethernet interfaces alongside the traditional 10 Mb/s interfaces.

Ethernet technology continues to evolve with new speeds, cabling types, and features. This RFC reflects the state of Ethernet management at the time (June 1998) and may be updated in the future as the technology advances. The MIB objects defined here let network administrators monitor the health and performance of Ethernet interfaces on managed devices.
sections.plainLanguage: This document describes what information a network device should give to a manager when asked about its Ethernet cables and connections.

sections.title: Interface Types and Relationships
sections.content:
The EtherLike-MIB applies to interfaces with the following types: ethernetCsmacd(6), iso88023Csmacd(7), and starLan(11). The RFC recommends that all Ethernet interfaces use ethernetCsmacd regardless of speed, since the actual speed can be determined from ifSpeed or ifHighSpeed objects in the Interfaces MIB.

The relationship between this MIB and others is important: it does not duplicate information already defined in MIB-2 or the Interfaces MIB (such as transmitted and received octets). Instead, it adds Ethernet-specific statistics. For managing duplex mode and media type, it requires support for the 802.3 MAU MIB. The RFC does not provide layering or support for sublayers, and Ethernet does not use virtual circuits.
sections.plainLanguage: This list of measurements fits with other SNMP measurements and refers to them when the information is already defined elsewhere.

sections.title: Interface Statistics and Error Monitoring
sections.content:
The dot3StatsTable is the core of this MIB module. It contains counters for each Ethernet interface, indexed by dot3StatsIndex (which matches the interface's ifIndex). Each row tracks the following statistics:

  • Alignment errors: Frames received that are not a whole number of octets and do not pass the Frame Check Sequence (FCS).
  • FCS errors: Frames that are correctly sized but fail the FCS check, indicating corruption.
  • Collision counts: Frames involved in single collisions, multiple collisions, late collisions, and excessive collisions.
  • Transmission errors: Deferred transmissions, carrier sense errors, and internal MAC transmit errors.
  • Reception errors: Frames too long for the maximum permitted size, and internal MAC receive errors.
  • SQE test errors: Signal Quality Errors detected by the Physical Layer Service (PLS).
  • Symbol errors: Invalid data symbols detected while a carrier was present (for 100 Mb/s interfaces).
  • Chipset identifier: An object identifier indicating which hardware chipset is used in the interface.

These counters help identify physical layer and media access problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Like a car's dashboard shows oil pressure and temperature, these counters show how many scrambled messages, crashes, and other problems happened on the cable.

sections.title: Collision Histograms and Diagnostics
sections.content:
The dot3CollTable provides a histogram of collisions per frame. For each interface, it tracks how many frames experienced exactly 1 collision, exactly 2 collisions, up to 16 collisions. This histogram helps diagnose whether collisions are rare (a sign of normal activity) or frequent (a sign of a congested or faulty network).

The RFC also defines two test types: TDR (Time-Domain Reflectometry) and Loopback. TDR is specific to coaxial Ethernet cables (10Base5 and 10Base2) and measures the distance to a cable fault by the time it takes for a reflected signal to return. Loopback tests the MAC chip's memory and logic by sending data through the interface's internal path. Note that the ifTestTable is deprecated in favor of new system testing mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a frame hits one collision, sometimes two, sometimes more. Keeping a tally of how many frames had how many collisions helps spot trouble.

sections.title: Chipset Identification and Implementation
sections.content:
The dot3StatsEtherChipSet object contains an identifier for the hardware chipset implementing the MAC (Media Access Control) functionality on an interface. The RFC registers identifiers for many common chipsets from vendors like AMD, Intel, SEEQ, National Semiconductor, and Fujitsu. This allows management stations to correlate statistics with known hardware anomalies and to understand the capabilities of managed interfaces.

For 100 Mb/s interfaces, the RFC defines two compliance statements: etherCompliance for interfaces running at 10 Mb/s or less, and ether100MbsCompliance for interfaces capable of 100 Mb/s. An interface that can run at 100 Mb/s must implement the 100 Mb/s compliance statement even if it is currently operating at a lower speed, with counters remaining zero when not in use.
sections.plainLanguage: Just as a mechanic might know that a certain car model has a transmission problem, managers can know that a certain chip might report incorrect statistics, so they can adjust accordingly.
